260.title: The Medina charter
260.hook: a written charter binds Muslims, Jews and others of the city in mutual defense
260.howItsDone: Muslims today use ummah above all for the worldwide community of believers, and some point to the Medina charter when they talk about how Muslims can live with neighbors of other faiths under shared promises.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ansar, the helpers of Medina who opened their homes. Your line was brothers by choice. Did you share something with someone new? Day two hundred sixty.

No police, no courts, no city council. Just families and clans, each with its own old grudges, and one newcomer they have agreed to listen to. Different languages in the lanes, different holidays, different loyalties, the same streets. Medina was a city like that. Arab clans, some of them Muslim now and some not. Jewish tribes who had lived there for generations. Newcomers from Mecca, with nothing. What do you do with a city like that? According to the early biographers, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had it written down. Today: ummah.
screen: `ONE STREET, MANY PEOPLES.` → `NO COURTS, OLD GRUDGES.` → `WRITTEN DOWN.`

segments.voice: The document is often called the Constitution of Medina, or the Medina charter. Its text comes to us through the early biographer Ibn Ishaq, and through another early scholar, Abu 'Ubayd. It's a list of agreements. Each clan pays its own blood money and ransoms its own captives, as before. Nobody shelters a murderer. If the city is attacked, everyone defends it together, and shares the cost. Disputes go to God and to Muhammad. And then the lines people still quote. The believers, from Mecca and from Medina, and those who join them and strive with them, are one ummah, one community, distinct from other people. And the Jews of one clan, the charter says, are an ummah alongside the believers: to the Jews their religion, and to the Muslims theirs. The word ummah comes from a root that also gives umm, mother, and imam, the one in front. An ummah is a people gathered around something at its center. In this document it's used in more than one way at once: the community of believers, and a wider civic community of the city, bound by promises. Historians who have studied it, such as R. B. Serjeant, treat it as early, and Serjeant argued it joins several agreements made at different times. And honesty matters here: relations with some of the Jewish tribes of Medina later broke down, and the path will come to that. But this day is about the beginning: one written page that tried to make one city out of many peoples.
screen: `A LIST OF PROMISES.` · `DEFEND THE CITY TOGETHER.` · `TO EACH THEIR RELIGION.` · `UMMAH — A PEOPLE AROUND A CENTER.` · then, large: `ONE CITY, MANY PEOPLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn your neighbors' names. Sit, and picture the people who live closest to you: next door, across the hall, above, below. For each one, ask yourself honestly whether you know their name. Just notice. No guilt. Then picture the one you'd most like to know, and the moment you might ask: at the mailbox, in the elevator, over the fence. If you pray, you can make du'a for them. The bell holds the time.
Ummah. A community, a people gathered around a center: in the charter, both the believers and the whole city bound by promises. Today's word.
Your line: one city, many peoples. Today, learn one neighbor's name, and use it. Day two hundred sixty.

261.title: The first adhan
261.hook: a companion dreams the call to prayer, and Bilal, with the best voice, calls it
261.howItsDone: The adhan is called before each of the five daily prayers, from mosques around the world, and many Muslims answer by repeating its words quietly as they hear them; Sunni and Shia adhans share most of their words, with some differences.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Medina charter, and the word ummah. Your line was one city, many peoples. Did you learn a neighbor's name? Day two hundred sixty-one.

There's a mosque now in Medina, mud walls and palm pillars. But there's a problem. Nobody has clocks. People are working in date groves, in the market, at home, and prayer time comes, and half of them miss it. So the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions sit down to solve it. How do you call a whole town together, five times a day? Someone suggests lighting a fire. Someone suggests a horn. Someone suggests striking a wooden clapper, the way their neighbors did. Nothing feels right. Then, one night, a man from Medina has a dream. And the answer, when it comes, isn't an instrument at all. It's a human voice. Today: adhan.
screen: `NO CLOCKS.` → `A FIRE? A HORN? A CLAPPER?` → `A DREAM.`

segments.voice: The man was Abdullah ibn Zayd. In the hadith, in the collections of Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, he dreams of a man carrying a wooden clapper, and asks to buy it, to call people to prayer. The man in the dream says, shall I show you something better? And he teaches him the words. Allahu akbar, God is greater, four times. I bear witness there is no god but God. I bear witness Muhammad is the messenger of God. Come to prayer. Come to success. God is greater. There is no god but God. In the morning Abdullah runs to the Prophet, who says: it's a true dream. Go and teach the words to Bilal, because his voice carries further than yours. And then Umar comes hurrying in, saying he dreamed the very same thing. Now, Bilal. Bilal ibn Rabah was an Abyssinian, a black African man who had been enslaved in Mecca. When he became Muslim, his master tortured him in the desert heat, with a heavy stone on his chest, to make him give it up. The early biographers say he just kept repeating one word, ahad, ahad, one, one. Abu Bakr bought his freedom. And now, in Medina, the Prophet chooses this man, formerly enslaved, from far away, to stand up and call the whole city to God. It's often said he'd climb onto the highest roof near the mosque at dawn to call. Muslims have called him the first mu'adhdhin ever since. Every adhan you hear anywhere in the world goes back to his voice.
screen: `ABDULLAH IBN ZAYD'S DREAM.` · `THE WORDS OF THE CALL.` · `HIS VOICE CARRIES FURTHER.` · `AHAD, AHAD.` · then, large: `BILAL CALLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to an adhan. If you can, find a recording now, from any mosque, any country, and just listen, all the way through. If you can't, sit quietly and imagine it: a single voice rising over rooftops before dawn, long notes, the same words for fourteen centuries. Notice how it starts: God is greater. Whatever you were doing, whatever you were worried about. God is greater. Let the sound settle into the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Adhan, the call to prayer: taught in a dream to Abdullah ibn Zayd, and first called out by Bilal.
Your line: bilal calls. Today, at one of the five prayer times, stop for ten seconds wherever you are, and imagine his voice reaching you. Day two hundred sixty-one.

262.title: The turning of the qiblah
262.hook: during a prayer the direction turns from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:144)
262.howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'ba in Mecca for each prayer, finding the direction by mosque niches, compasses or phone apps, and the mosque of the two qiblahs in Medina is visited by many pilgrims.

segments.voice: Yesterday, adhan, and Bilal's voice over the rooftops. Your line was bilal calls. Did you stop, even for ten seconds, at a prayer time? Day two hundred sixty-two.

A small mosque on the edge of Medina. A row of men are in the middle of the afternoon prayer, facing north, toward Jerusalem, the way Muslims have prayed for years. Someone comes in at the door. He's just prayed with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and he calls out: the direction has changed. We've been told to face the Ka'ba in Mecca. And the whole row, in the middle of the prayer, without breaking it, turns around. North to south. Their backs are now where their faces were. A mosque in Medina today carries a name that remembers it: the mosque of the two qiblahs. Today: qiblah.
screen: `MID-PRAYER, FACING JERUSALEM.` → `THE DIRECTION HAS CHANGED.` → `THE WHOLE ROW TURNS.`

segments.voice: The qiblah is the direction Muslims face in prayer. For the first years, including about sixteen or seventeen months in Medina, Sahih al-Bukhari says, the Prophet and his companions prayed toward Jerusalem, toward the holy house there. Commentators connect it with the long line of prophets before him, Abraham, Moses, David, Jesus, whom Muslims count as prophets too. But the hadith says he longed to face the Ka'ba, the house the Qur'an says Abraham and Ishmael raised. The Qur'an describes him turning his face to the sky, and then the verse came, in al-Baqarah: turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. Some people objected. Why change? And the Qur'an's answer, two verses earlier, in Pickthall's words, is: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West." Muslim teachers draw the lesson plainly: the direction was never where God is. The qiblah is where the community faces, together, so that people in every place line up toward one point. The next verse adds that the change was also a test: would people follow, even when it was hard to understand? Some followed in the middle of a prayer. And a detail worth keeping: the Qur'an itself says elsewhere that goodness isn't just turning your face east or west, but faith and generosity and keeping your word. The direction matters. It was never the whole thing.
screen: `FIRST, TOWARD JERUSALEM.` · `TURN YOUR FACE TO THE SACRED MOSQUE.` · `EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD.` · `NOT ONLY WHICH WAY YOU FACE.` · then, large: `TURN YOUR FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face the qiblah once more. If you know the direction of Mecca from where you are, or can find it on your phone, turn and face it now. Sit, or stand. People praying anywhere on earth face this same point, from every side, like the spokes of a wheel. If you don't know the direction, just turn slowly in a full circle, and recall the verse: unto Allah belong the East and the West. Then sit, facing that way. The bell holds the time.
Qiblah, the direction faced in prayer: changed from Jerusalem to the Ka'ba in Mecca, remembered as a row turning mid-prayer.
Your line: turn your face. Today, when you catch yourself facing the wrong way, toward a grudge or a screen or a worry, turn, physically if it helps. Day two hundred sixty-two.

263.title: Fasting is prescribed
263.hook: the fast of Ramadan is ordained in the second year (2:183)
263.howItsDone: Muslims fast every day of Ramadan from dawn to sunset, with a pre-dawn meal (suhur) and a meal at sunset (iftar); the sick, travelers, and others excused make up the days later or feed the poor, and some also fast voluntarily on Mondays and Thursdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qiblah, a whole row turning mid-prayer. Your line was turn your face. What did you turn away from, and toward? Day two hundred sixty-three.

Before dawn, a quick meal in a quiet kitchen. Then nothing to eat or drink until sunset. Office workers in London. Farmers in Indonesia. Students in Chicago, slipping out of a lecture to break the fast with a date and a bottle of water. Grandmothers cooking all afternoon for food they can't taste yet. Every Ramadan, a month of days like that. But it had a first year. In Medina, after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ arrived, a verse came down that started all of it. Today: kutiba.
screen: `A MONTH, DAWN TO SUNSET.` → `A DATE AND WATER AT SUNSET.` → `IT HAD A FIRST YEAR.`

segments.voice: The verse is in al-Baqarah. In Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." Three things in that one line. Prescribed: kutiba, written. Fasting was written for them, the way a rule is written down. Before you: this isn't new, the verse says; it was prescribed for those before. In fact, before Ramadan, the Prophet had fasted on the day of 'Ashura, and Sahih al-Bukhari says the Jews of Medina fasted that day too, remembering Moses being saved. After Ramadan was prescribed, 'Ashura stayed as a fast people could choose. And the reason: that you may ward off evil, or as it's often explained, that you may gain taqwa, the careful awareness of God we've met before. Teachers often explain that the fast isn't about hunger for its own sake. It's practice in saying no to what you want, so you can say no to worse things. The next verses fill in the kindness. It's a fixed number of days. If you're sick or traveling, make the days up later. And the verses speak of feeding a poor person as a ransom, which scholars apply to those who can't fast at all. And then the line: God wants ease for you, not hardship. The month is Ramadan, the verses say, the month in which the Qur'an was sent down. Tradition dates this command to the second year after the migration. So the very first Ramadan fast happened in that plain little city, in a mosque of palm trunks.
screen: `KUTIBA — WRITTEN FOR YOU.` · `AS FOR THOSE BEFORE YOU.` · `THAT YOU MAY WARD OFF EVIL.` · `EASE, NOT HARDSHIP.` · then, large: `PRESCRIBED FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one voluntary fast. Only if fasting is safe for your body; the verses themselves excuse the sick. At-Tirmidhi records that the Prophet made a habit of fasting on Mondays and Thursdays, and some Muslims keep it. Sit, and pick a day. Picture the pre-dawn meal, the long afternoon, the first sip of water at sunset. If a food fast isn't right for you, pick one thing to go without from dawn to sunset. The bell holds the time.
Kutiba, it is written: the word in 2:183 that wrote the fast of Ramadan for Muslims, as it was written for those before them.
Your line: prescribed for you. Today, put the fast day you chose in your calendar, and tell one person. Day two hundred sixty-three.

264.title: The wells of Badr
264.hook: a small, outnumbered band of Muslims meets the Meccan army by the wells of Badr, and wins
264.howItsDone: Some Muslims mark the battle of Badr in Ramadan with talks in mosques about the people who took part, whom later generations honored as the people of Badr.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kutiba, the first Ramadan in Medina. Your line was prescribed for you. Did you put a fast day on your calendar? Day two hundred sixty-four.

It's that same first Ramadan. And word comes that a large army has marched out of Mecca, the city that drove them out, about a thousand men, with horses and armor. The Muslims who ride out to meet them number a little over three hundred. The biographers say they have two horses between them, and about seventy camels, taking turns riding. Some have no armor at all. They camp near a group of wells in a valley called Badr, on the caravan road southwest of Medina. The night before, it rains. The next morning, the two sides face each other across the sand. Today: Badr.
screen: `A THOUSAND FROM MECCA.` → `THREE HUNDRED AND SOME.` → `A VALLEY OF WELLS.`

segments.voice: Two moments before the battle are worth knowing. The first is about the wells, and it comes from the early biographer Ibn Ishaq. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stopped the army at one spot. A companion named al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir came to him and asked, politely: is this place one God has shown you, or is it your own judgment, a matter of war and planning? The Prophet said it was his own judgment. Then, said al-Hubab, this isn't the right place. Let's move to the well nearest the enemy, build a cistern, and keep the water on our side. And the Prophet said: you've given good advice, and moved the whole army. A prophet, taking correction from a soldier, in front of everyone. The second moment is the night. Sahih Muslim describes the Prophet standing in prayer, hands raised, calling on God so long and so hard that his cloak slipped off his shoulders, and Abu Bakr put it back and told him, enough, God will keep his promise to you. Then the battle. The Meccans broke. Sahih al-Bukhari counts seventy of them killed and seventy taken captive, among the dead several of the leaders who had tormented the Muslims in Mecca. The biographers name about fourteen Muslims who died. The Qur'an looks back on it later: God had already helped you at Badr, when you were weak and few. It says the Muslims were strengthened with angels, and it says the victory was God's, not theirs. Muslim teachers often tell Badr not as a story about strength, but about the opposite: how little they had, and how much came through anyway.
screen: `YOUR JUDGMENT, OR GOD'S?` · `MOVE TO THE NEAREST WELL.` · `HIS CLOAK SLIPPED IN PRAYER.` · `WHEN YOU WERE WEAK AND FEW.` · then, large: `FEW AGAINST MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember an unlikely rescue. Sit, and go back in your own life to a time when the odds were against you. Not enough money, not enough time, not enough strength. And somehow, you got through. A stranger's help. A door that opened at the last minute. Let the memory come back in detail: where you were, what you felt. Then notice how little you actually had then. If you pray, you can thank God for it. The bell holds the time.
Badr, the valley where a small, outnumbered band of Muslims met the Meccan army in the first Ramadan, and won.
Your line: few against many. Today, when something feels too big for what you've got, remember the three hundred, and take the next step anyway. Day two hundred sixty-four.

265.title: Mercy to captives
265.hook: the prisoners of Badr are fed well, and some freed for teaching Muslim children to read
265.howItsDone: Muslims often cite the captives of Badr and Qur'an 76:8 when teaching about the humane treatment of prisoners, and the ransom of literacy is remembered as an early honoring of learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Badr, three hundred against a thousand. Your line was few against many. Did you take one step on something that felt too big? Day two hundred sixty-five.

The battle is over. And now the Muslims of Medina have something they've never had before: about seventy prisoners. These are men from Mecca, some of whom had mocked them, boycotted them, driven them from their homes. Some are relatives: cousins, brothers, an uncle. In that world, a captive's life was in his captor's hands. The prisoners are marched back to Medina, tied up, and divided among Muslim households to be held until their families can pay a ransom. What would you expect? What happened next surprised even the prisoners. Today: mercy to captives.
screen: `SEVENTY PRISONERS.` → `THE MEN WHO DROVE THEM OUT.` → `WHAT WOULD YOU EXPECT?`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions to treat the captives well. And the early biographer Ibn Ishaq keeps the memory of one prisoner, Abu 'Aziz, who described it afterward. He said the family of Ansar holding him would give him the bread, which was the better food, and eat only dates themselves, because of what the Prophet had told them. He said he'd hand the bread back, embarrassed, and they'd give it right back to him. Food was not plentiful in Medina. They gave the enemy the good part. The Qur'an praises this kind of thing elsewhere: the righteous feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, for the love of God, wanting no reward and no thanks. Then there was the ransom. Families in Mecca paid to free their men. But some prisoners were poor, and had no one to pay. And a report from Ibn 'Abbas, in the Musnad of Ahmad, says the Prophet set a different price for some of them: teach the children of the Ansar to write, and you're free. Later tellings say ten children each. A young community, fighting for its life, and what it asks of its enemies is literacy for its kids. Tradition says one of the children who learned to write this way was Zayd ibn Thabit, who would later become one of the main scribes of the Qur'an. And one more detail: the Prophet's own uncle, al-'Abbas, was among the captives. Ibn Sa'd says the Prophet couldn't sleep that night, hearing him groan in his ropes, until they were loosened.
screen: `THEY GAVE THE ENEMY THE BREAD.` · `FOR THE LOVE OF GOD, NO THANKS.` · `TEACH THE CHILDREN TO WRITE.` · `ZAYD, THE FUTURE SCRIBE.` · then, large: `FREEDOM FOR TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach someone something. Sit, and think of one thing you know how to do that someone near you doesn't. How to cook a dish. How to change a tire. A phrase in another language. A shortcut on the computer. How to make wudu, if that's yours to teach. Picture the person, and the moment you'd show them, patiently, the way the prisoners of Badr taught children to shape their letters. The bell holds the time.
Mercy to captives. After Badr, prisoners were fed with the better food, and some were freed for teaching Muslim children to read and write. Today's word.
Your line: freedom for teaching. Today, teach that one small thing to someone, and let them keep it. Day two hundred sixty-five.

266.title: The hill at Uhud
266.hook: the archers leave the hill, the battle turns, and the Prophet ﷺ is wounded
266.howItsDone: Pilgrims to Medina visit Mount Uhud and the small archers' hill beside it, often called Jabal ar-Rumah, and Muslim teachers tell the story as a lesson in obedience and staying at one's post.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy to captives, bread for the enemy and freedom for teaching. Your line was freedom for teaching. What did you teach, and to whom? Day two hundred sixty-six, the end of a week.

A year after Badr, Mecca comes back, and this time it's ready. Three thousand men march on Medina. The Muslims, about seven hundred after a group turns back, meet them at the foot of a mountain just north of the city, Uhud. Beside the battlefield is a small hill. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ puts fifty archers on it, under a companion named 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr, to guard the Muslims' back from the enemy's horsemen. And he gives them an order so clear it's hard to misread. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it: even if you see birds snatching us up, don't leave your place until I send for you. Today: Uhud.
screen: `THREE THOUSAND FROM MECCA.` → `FIFTY ARCHERS ON A HILL.` → `DON'T LEAVE YOUR PLACE.`

segments.voice: At first the battle goes the Muslims' way. The Meccan lines break. Their camp is left open, full of goods. And up on the hill the archers watch their friends below gathering the spoils, and they start saying: it's over, we've won, let's go down. 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr reminds them of the order. Most of them go anyway. He stays, with fewer than ten. Watching from the Meccan side is a cavalry commander named Khalid ibn al-Walid. He sees the hill empty, circles around behind it, and charges into the Muslims' backs. Everything turns. The men left on the hill are killed. The Muslim ranks scatter. The Prophet himself is struck. Sahih Muslim says his tooth was broken and his face was cut, and he wiped away the blood. Word spreads across the field that he's been killed, and some fighters simply drop their swords and sit down. Later the Qur'an speaks to them directly, and it doesn't flatter them. God kept his promise to you, it says, until you lost heart, and quarreled over the order, and disobeyed, after he'd shown you what you loved. Some of you wanted this world. And to those who panicked at the rumor: Muhammad is only a messenger, and messengers have passed away before him. Will you turn back on your heels? And then, remarkably, it says God has forgiven them. The lesson Muslims draw is simple and hard: hold the post you were given, even when it looks like the job is done. Look back at this week: an ummah, a call, a turning, a fast, a victory, a mercy, and now a hill left too soon.
screen: `IT'S OVER, LET'S GO DOWN.` · `KHALID SEES THE EMPTY HILL.` · `THE PROPHET IS WOUNDED.` · `YOU LOST HEART, AND FORGIVEN.` · then, large: `HOLD THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep your post today. Sit, and ask: what's my hill? The thing I've been trusted with that's easy to walk away from once it looks finished. A promise to a friend. A shift at work. A child's homework. A habit you started on this path. Picture the moment you're most likely to leave it early, when it seems like nobody would notice. Now picture yourself staying. The bell holds the time.
Uhud, the mountain just north of Medina where fifty archers were told never to leave a hill, and most left, and the battle turned.
Your line: hold the hill. Today, finish the one thing you're tempted to leave early, all the way to the end. Day two hundred sixty-six.
